question: Give me a list of AIGA Medal awardees awarded from 2022 to 2014 who were awarded posthumously 20 years or more after their death. In the case of someone dying in the same year that the award is given, treat this as not posthumous. If two people were given a joint medal, if either one of them died prior then you should treat this as posthumous, and you should list the entry as a single entry for any joint awardees. Present the list in alphabetical order by first name.
gold_answer:
Aaron Douglas
Alexander Girard
Corita Kent
Dan Friedman

answer:
**AIGA Medal recipients (2022 – 2014) who were honored post‑humously **20 years or more** after their death**

| Year awarded | Recipient | Year of death | Years between death and award |
|--------------|-----------|--------------|------------------------------|
| 2018 | **Aaron Douglas** | 1990 | 28 years |
| 2019 | **Alexander Girard** | 1993 | 26 years |
| 2016 | **Corita Kent** | 1986 | 30 years |

*Order is alphabetical by first name (Aaron, Alexander, Corita). No joint‑award entries are involved, so each recipient is listed individually.*

steps.reasoning:
We need to list AIGA Medal awardees from 2022 to 2014 (inclusive). We need posthumous awards that are at least 20 years after death. If death same year award, not posthumous. Joint medals: if either died prior, treat as posthumous, list as single entry. Alphabetically by first name.

We need to identify awardees from those years, and see who died over 20 years earlier. Let's search.

**2017** (MMXVII) was a common year starting on Sunday of the Gregorian calendar, the 2017th year of the Common Era (CE) and _Anno Domini_ (AD) designations, the 17th year of the 3rd millenniumand the 21st century, and the 8th year of the 2010s decade.
2017 was designated as the International Year of Sustainable Tourism for Development by the United Nations General Assembly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-1)

*   January 1 – Istanbul nightclub shooting: A gunman dressed as Santa Claus opens fire at the Reina nightclub in Istanbul, Turkey, killing 39 people and injuring 79 others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-2)  
*   January 8 – 2017 Jerusalem truck attack: A Palestinian assailant entered the road where the Israeli defense forces were located with a truck, killing 4 people and injuring 15 others.  
*   January 16 – Turkish Airlines Flight 6491, a cargo flight en route from Hong Kong to Istanbul via Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, crashes in a residential area while attempting to land at Manas International Airport, Bishkek, killing all four crew members on board and 35 people on the ground.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-3)  
*   January 19 – 2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) launches a military intervention in the Gambia after Yahya Jammeh refuses to cede power following the 2016 presidential elections.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-4)  
*   January 21  
    *   2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis: Following the military intervention of ECOWAS, PresidentYahya Jammeh resigns from office after 23 years in power and flees into exile to Equatorial Guinea; the democratically elected Adama Barrow assumes office as President of The Gambia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-ReutersFlies-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-JammehLeavesBBC-6)  

    *   Millions of people worldwide join the [Women's March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Women's_March "2017 Women's March") following the inauguration of Donald Trump as President of the United States. 420 marches were reported in the U.S. and 168 in other countries, becoming the largest single-day protest in American history at the time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-7)
*   January 27 – U.S. President Donald Trump issues executive order banning travel and immigration from seven Muslim-majority nations. Protests against the immigration order erupt nationwide for about two weeks.  
*   January 29 – A gunman opens fire at a mosque in Quebec City, Canada, killing 6 and injuring 19 others.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-9)  
*   January 30 – Morocco rejoins the African Union.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-10)
"February 2017" redirects here. For the Charli XCX song, see Charli (album).

*   August 18 – The first terrorist attack ever sentenced as a crime in Finland kills two people and injures eight others. Islamic terrorist Abderrahman Bouanane, a Moroccan man carried out the ISIS-inspired attack in southwest Finland.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-52)  
*   August 21 – A total solar eclipse (nicknamed "The Great American Eclipse")[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-53) is visible within a band across the entire contiguous United States of America, passing from the Pacific to the Atlantic coasts. The moon was just 3 days past perigee, making it relatively large.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-56)  
*   August 25–ongoing – A military operation targeting Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar "seems a textbook example of ethnic cleansing", according to the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-57)  
*   August 25–30 – Hurricane Harvey strikes the United States as a Category 4 hurricane, causing catastrophic damage to the Houston metropolitan area, mostly due to record-breaking floods. At least 108 deaths are recorded, and total damage reaches $125 billion (2017 USD), making Harvey the costliest natural disaster in United States history, tied with Hurricane Katrina in 2005.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-TCR-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-NOAACostliest-59)

*   September 1 – Russian PresidentVladimir Putin expels 755 diplomats in response to United Statessanctions.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-60)  
*   United States Passports become invalid to travel to North Korea, in response to the death of Otto Warmbier.  
*   September 3 – North Korea conducts its sixth and most powerful nuclear test.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-61)  
*   September 6 – Hurricane Irma, at peak intensity, would make the first of many powerful landfalls along the Caribbean islands and the United States. Damages would total $77.2 billion (2017 USD), and 134 would be killed by the storm.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-62)  
*   September 13 – The International Olympic Committee awards Paris and Los Angeles the right to host the 2024 and 2028 Summer Olympics, respectively.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-63)  
*   September 15 – _Cassini–Huygens_ ends its 13-year mission by plunging into Saturn, becoming the first spacecraft to enter the planet's atmosphere.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-Cassini-64)  
*   September 19 – Twelve days after another powerful earthquake, and on the 32nd anniversary of the deadly 1985 Mexico City earthquake, a 7.1 M wearthquake strikes central Mexico, killing 370, leaving up to 6,000 injured[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-CBSMexicoCity-65) and thousands more homeless.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-McDonnell-66)  

*   September 19–20 – Just two weeks after Hurricane Irma struck the Caribbean, Hurricane Maria strikes similar areas, making landfall on Dominica as a Category 5 hurricane, and Puerto Rico as a Category 4 hurricane. Maria caused over 3,000 deaths and damages estimated in excess of $91.6 billion (2017 USD).[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-NOAACostliest-59)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-auto-67)  
*   September 25 – The Kurdistan Regionvotes in a referendum to become an independent state, in defiance of Iraq;[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-68) by October 15, the crisis escalates into a short-lived armed conflict over disputed territories.  
*   September 26 – _Fortnite Battle Royale_ releases, becoming one of the biggest video games in the world and a cultural phenomenon.

*   October 1 – 60 people are killed and 867 more injured when Stephen Paddockopens fire on a crowd in Las Vegas, surpassing the 2016 Orlando nightclub shooting as the deadliest mass shooting perpetrated by a lone gunman in U.S. history.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-LVS-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-59th_Victim-70)  
*   October 12 – The United States announces its decision to withdraw from UNESCO,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-71) and is immediately followed by Israel.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-72)  
*   October 14 – A massive blast caused by a truck bombing in Mogadishu, Somalia kills at least 587 people and injures 316 others.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-73)  
*   October 16 - Maltese investigative journalist and blogger Daphne Caruana Galizia is killed by a car bomb outside her home in Bidnija.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-75)  
*   October 17 – Syrian Civil War: Raqqa is declared fully liberated from the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant.  
*   October 25 – At the 19th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, Xi Jinping assumes his second term as General Secretary (China's paramount leader), and the political theory Xi Jinping Thought is written into the party's constitution.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-76)  

*   October 26 – At the level crossing of the Hanko–Hyvinkää railway line, a passenger train collided with an off-road truck of the Nyland Brigade in Raseborg, Finland; four people died and 11 were injured.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-78)  
*   October 27 – Based on the results of a previously held referendum, Catalonia declares independence from Spain,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-79) but the Catalan Republic is not recognised by the Spanish government or any other sovereign nation.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-80)

**2017** (MMXVII) was a common year starting on Sunday of the Gregorian calendar, the 2017th year of the Common Era (CE) and _Anno Domini_ (AD) designations, the 17th year of the 3rd millenniumand the 21st century, and the 8th year of the 2010s decade.
2017 was designated as the International Year of Sustainable Tourism for Development by the United Nations General Assembly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-1)
texts.3:
*   January 1 – Istanbul nightclub shooting: A gunman dressed as Santa Claus opens fire at the Reina nightclub in Istanbul, Turkey, killing 39 people and injuring 79 others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-2)  
*   January 8 – 2017 Jerusalem truck attack: A Palestinian assailant entered the road where the Israeli defense forces were located with a truck, killing 4 people and injuring 15 others.  
*   January 16 – Turkish Airlines Flight 6491, a cargo flight en route from Hong Kong to Istanbul via Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, crashes in a residential area while attempting to land at Manas International Airport, Bishkek, killing all four crew members on board and 35 people on the ground.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-3)  
*   January 19 – 2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) launches a military intervention in the Gambia after Yahya Jammeh refuses to cede power following the 2016 presidential elections.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-4)  
*   January 21  
    *   2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis: Following the military intervention of ECOWAS, PresidentYahya Jammeh resigns from office after 23 years in power and flees into exile to Equatorial Guinea; the democratically elected Adama Barrow assumes office as President of The Gambia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-ReutersFlies-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-JammehLeavesBBC-6)
texts.4:
*   Millions of people worldwide join the [Women's March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Women's_March "2017 Women's March") following the inauguration of Donald Trump as President of the United States. 420 marches were reported in the U.S. and 168 in other countries, becoming the largest single-day protest in American history at the time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-7)
*   January 27 – U.S. President Donald Trump issues executive order banning travel and immigration from seven Muslim-majority nations. Protests against the immigration order erupt nationwide for about two weeks.  
*   January 29 – A gunman opens fire at a mosque in Quebec City, Canada, killing 6 and injuring 19 others.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-9)  
*   January 30 – Morocco rejoins the African Union.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-10)
"February 2017" redirects here. For the Charli XCX song, see Charli (album).
texts.13:
*   August 18 – The first terrorist attack ever sentenced as a crime in Finland kills two people and injures eight others. Islamic terrorist Abderrahman Bouanane, a Moroccan man carried out the ISIS-inspired attack in southwest Finland.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-52)  
*   August 21 – A total solar eclipse (nicknamed "The Great American Eclipse")[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-53) is visible within a band across the entire contiguous United States of America, passing from the Pacific to the Atlantic coasts. The moon was just 3 days past perigee, making it relatively large.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-56)  
*   August 25–ongoing – A military operation targeting Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar "seems a textbook example of ethnic cleansing", according to the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-57)  
*   August 25–30 – Hurricane Harvey strikes the United States as a Category 4 hurricane, causing catastrophic damage to the Houston metropolitan area, mostly due to record-breaking floods. At least 108 deaths are recorded, and total damage reaches $125 billion (2017 USD), making Harvey the costliest natural disaster in United States history, tied with Hurricane Katrina in 2005.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-TCR-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-NOAACostliest-59)
texts.14:
*   September 1 – Russian PresidentVladimir Putin expels 755 diplomats in response to United Statessanctions.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-60)  
*   United States Passports become invalid to travel to North Korea, in response to the death of Otto Warmbier.  
*   September 3 – North Korea conducts its sixth and most powerful nuclear test.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-61)  
*   September 6 – Hurricane Irma, at peak intensity, would make the first of many powerful landfalls along the Caribbean islands and the United States. Damages would total $77.2 billion (2017 USD), and 134 would be killed by the storm.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-62)  
*   September 13 – The International Olympic Committee awards Paris and Los Angeles the right to host the 2024 and 2028 Summer Olympics, respectively.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-63)  
*   September 15 – _Cassini–Huygens_ ends its 13-year mission by plunging into Saturn, becoming the first spacecraft to enter the planet's atmosphere.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-Cassini-64)  
*   September 19 – Twelve days after another powerful earthquake, and on the 32nd anniversary of the deadly 1985 Mexico City earthquake, a 7.1 M wearthquake strikes central Mexico, killing 370, leaving up to 6,000 injured[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-CBSMexicoCity-65) and thousands more homeless.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-McDonnell-66)
texts.15:
*   September 19–20 – Just two weeks after Hurricane Irma struck the Caribbean, Hurricane Maria strikes similar areas, making landfall on Dominica as a Category 5 hurricane, and Puerto Rico as a Category 4 hurricane. Maria caused over 3,000 deaths and damages estimated in excess of $91.6 billion (2017 USD).[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-NOAACostliest-59)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-auto-67)  
*   September 25 – The Kurdistan Regionvotes in a referendum to become an independent state, in defiance of Iraq;[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-68) by October 15, the crisis escalates into a short-lived armed conflict over disputed territories.  
*   September 26 – _Fortnite Battle Royale_ releases, becoming one of the biggest video games in the world and a cultural phenomenon.
texts.16:
*   October 1 – 60 people are killed and 867 more injured when Stephen Paddockopens fire on a crowd in Las Vegas, surpassing the 2016 Orlando nightclub shooting as the deadliest mass shooting perpetrated by a lone gunman in U.S. history.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-LVS-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-59th_Victim-70)  
*   October 12 – The United States announces its decision to withdraw from UNESCO,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-71) and is immediately followed by Israel.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-72)  
*   October 14 – A massive blast caused by a truck bombing in Mogadishu, Somalia kills at least 587 people and injures 316 others.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-73)  
*   October 16 - Maltese investigative journalist and blogger Daphne Caruana Galizia is killed by a car bomb outside her home in Bidnija.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-75)  
*   October 17 – Syrian Civil War: Raqqa is declared fully liberated from the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant.  
*   October 25 – At the 19th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, Xi Jinping assumes his second term as General Secretary (China's paramount leader), and the political theory Xi Jinping Thought is written into the party's constitution.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-76)
texts.17:
*   October 26 – At the level crossing of the Hanko–Hyvinkää railway line, a passenger train collided with an off-road truck of the Nyland Brigade in Raseborg, Finland; four people died and 11 were injured.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-78)  
*   October 27 – Based on the results of a previously held referendum, Catalonia declares independence from Spain,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-79) but the Catalan Republic is not recognised by the Spanish government or any other sovereign nation.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-80)

**2017** (MMXVII) was a common year starting on Sunday of the Gregorian calendar, the 2017th year of the Common Era (CE) and _Anno Domini_ (AD) designations, the 17th year of the 3rd millenniumand the 21st century, and the 8th year of the 2010s decade.
2017 was designated as the International Year of Sustainable Tourism for Development by the United Nations General Assembly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-1)

*   January 1 – Istanbul nightclub shooting: A gunman dressed as Santa Claus opens fire at the Reina nightclub in Istanbul, Turkey, killing 39 people and injuring 79 others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-2)  
*   January 8 – 2017 Jerusalem truck attack: A Palestinian assailant entered the road where the Israeli defense forces were located with a truck, killing 4 people and injuring 15 others.  
*   January 16 – Turkish Airlines Flight 6491, a cargo flight en route from Hong Kong to Istanbul via Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, crashes in a residential area while attempting to land at Manas International Airport, Bishkek, killing all four crew members on board and 35 people on the ground.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-3)  
*   January 19 – 2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) launches a military intervention in the Gambia after Yahya Jammeh refuses to cede power following the 2016 presidential elections.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-4)  
*   January 21  
    *   2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis: Following the military intervention of ECOWAS, PresidentYahya Jammeh resigns from office after 23 years in power and flees into exile to Equatorial Guinea; the democratically elected Adama Barrow assumes office as President of The Gambia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-ReutersFlies-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-JammehLeavesBBC-6)  

    *   Millions of people worldwide join the [Women's March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Women's_March "2017 Women's March") following the inauguration of Donald Trump as President of the United States. 420 marches were reported in the U.S. and 168 in other countries, becoming the largest single-day protest in American history at the time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-7)
*   January 27 – U.S. President Donald Trump issues executive order banning travel and immigration from seven Muslim-majority nations. Protests against the immigration order erupt nationwide for about two weeks.  
*   January 29 – A gunman opens fire at a mosque in Quebec City, Canada, killing 6 and injuring 19 others.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-9)  
*   January 30 – Morocco rejoins the African Union.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-10)

*   August 21 – A total solar eclipse (nicknamed "The Great American Eclipse")[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-53) is visible within a band across the entire contiguous United States of America, passing from the Pacific to the Atlantic coasts. The moon was just 3 days past perigee, making it relatively large.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-56)  
*   August 25–ongoing – A military operation targeting Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar "seems a textbook example of ethnic cleansing", according to the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-57)  
*   August 25–30 – Hurricane Harvey strikes the United States as a Category 4 hurricane, causing catastrophic damage to the Houston metropolitan area, mostly due to record-breaking floods. At least 108 deaths are recorded, and total damage reaches $125 billion (2017 USD), making Harvey the costliest natural disaster in United States history, tied with Hurricane Katrina in 2005.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-TCR-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-NOAACostliest-59)

*   September 1 – Russian PresidentVladimir Putin expels 755 diplomats in response to United Statessanctions.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-60)  
*   United States Passports become invalid to travel to North Korea, in response to the death of Otto Warmbier.  
*   September 3 – North Korea conducts its sixth and most powerful nuclear test.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-61)  
*   September 6 – Hurricane Irma, at peak intensity, would make the first of many powerful landfalls along the Caribbean islands and the United States. Damages would total $77.2 billion (2017 USD), and 134 would be killed by the storm.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-62)  
*   September 13 – The International Olympic Committee awards Paris and Los Angeles the right to host the 2024 and 2028 Summer Olympics, respectively.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-63)  
*   September 15 – _Cassini–Huygens_ ends its 13-year mission by plunging into Saturn, becoming the first spacecraft to enter the planet's atmosphere.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-Cassini-64)  
*   September 19 – Twelve days after another powerful earthquake, and on the 32nd anniversary of the deadly 1985 Mexico City earthquake, a 7.1 M wearthquake strikes central Mexico, killing 370, leaving up to 6,000 injured[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-CBSMexicoCity-65) and thousands more homeless.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-McDonnell-66)  

*   September 19–20 – Just two weeks after Hurricane Irma struck the Caribbean, Hurricane Maria strikes similar areas, making landfall on Dominica as a Category 5 hurricane, and Puerto Rico as a Category 4 hurricane. Maria caused over 3,000 deaths and damages estimated in excess of $91.6 billion (2017 USD).[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-NOAACostliest-59)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-auto-67)  
*   September 25 – The Kurdistan Regionvotes in a referendum to become an independent state, in defiance of Iraq;[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-68) by October 15, the crisis escalates into a short-lived armed conflict over disputed territories.  
*   September 26 – _Fortnite Battle Royale_ releases, becoming one of the biggest video games in the world and a cultural phenomenon.

*   October 1 – 60 people are killed and 867 more injured when Stephen Paddockopens fire on a crowd in Las Vegas, surpassing the 2016 Orlando nightclub shooting as the deadliest mass shooting perpetrated by a lone gunman in U.S. history.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-LVS-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-59th_Victim-70)  
*   October 12 – The United States announces its decision to withdraw from UNESCO,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-71) and is immediately followed by Israel.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-72)  
*   October 14 – A massive blast caused by a truck bombing in Mogadishu, Somalia kills at least 587 people and injures 316 others.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-73)  
*   October 16 - Maltese investigative journalist and blogger Daphne Caruana Galizia is killed by a car bomb outside her home in Bidnija.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-75)  
*   October 17 – Syrian Civil War: Raqqa is declared fully liberated from the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant.  
*   October 25 – At the 19th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, Xi Jinping assumes his second term as General Secretary (China's paramount leader), and the political theory Xi Jinping Thought is written into the party's constitution.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-76)  

*   October 26 – At the level crossing of the Hanko–Hyvinkää railway line, a passenger train collided with an off-road truck of the Nyland Brigade in Raseborg, Finland; four people died and 11 were injured.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-78)  
*   October 27 – Based on the results of a previously held referendum, Catalonia declares independence from Spain,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-79) but the Catalan Republic is not recognised by the Spanish government or any other sovereign nation.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017#cite_note-80)

Title: AIGA Design Conference 2022: the award medalists, the hosts, the talks and design’s audacious future - TypeRoom
Chunks: 0,1,2
Just a few days after Inscipt Experimental Type Festival (available to revisit under Replay mode for ticket holders only), another celebration of contemporary design kicks off in search of the creative industry’s next frontier, enter theAIGADesign Conference 2022 October 20-22.
A gathering “for the diverse and ever-changing design community to gather together, inspire and explore how design can and will change the future” for 2022, AIGA Design Conference draws its focus on “Re-Connecting” with its community as the first after a three years hiatus in-person AIGA conference, with a virtual option also available.
Aiming to “celebrate the contributions and impact of design” and searching for design’s next frontiers. AIGA Design Conference 2022 introduces “a new twist to our mainstage” by welcoming three hosts to guide the ticket holders “through the most pressing, cutting edge, and provocative topics impacting design.”
AIGA’s Conference chair akaMATTER’s Rick Griffith, along with Brian Collins of COLLINS,Debbie Millman, andLee-Sean Huang, are the moderators who aim to lead “insightful discussions about the impact of design on our world.”
Bringing together a diverse roster of speakers working in “bold new ways, and exploring how design can build better bridges” AIGA Design Conference 2022 will look past the looking glass addressing “the world’s newest challenges, and learn how we can all make positive progress” through design.
Highlights include the Fireside Chats session and the AIGA Awards Celebration. Hosted by AIGA’s executive director Bennie F. Johnson the Fireside Chats’ theme is the future of design, with guests Audrey Lui, VP, head of design at Lyft,Tim Allen, global head of design at Instacart,Arem Duplessis, Apple’s group creative director and Pepsi’s chief design officer Mauro Porcini.
The recipients of this year’s AIGA Award, are designers and practitioners highly influential in the design industry. This year’s recipients areAndrew Satake Blauvelt,Emily Oberman, andLouise Sandhaus.
Video 3

Blauvelt is a designer, curator, historian, critic, and educator whose practice spans the fields of art and culture. Since 2015, he has served as Director of Cranbrook Art Museum in metropolitan Detroit leading the institution’s transformation into a vibrant and diverse cultural destination and community partner. Having studied and practiced graphic design, Blauvelt has expanded his practice to also include authoring historical research; curating major exhibitions on art, architecture, and design; editorial design for both print and online publishing; conceiving and managing strategic design initiatives; and writing theory and criticism about the field.⁠ AIGA recognizes Blauvelt “for his vast work in the field of art and design in service of the public — a steward of design history, he has redefined the traditional role of the museum in the community and made innovative cultural and educational programming accessible to all.”⁠
Emily Oberman is a multidisciplinary designer whose work spans brand identity, motion graphics, publications, packaging, advertising, and digital. She has been a partner in the New York office of the international design consultancyPentagram design since 2012. ⁠AIGA recognizes Oberman “for imprinting our visual culture with her wit and great fluency of style — highly influential, she is a north star for designers in the business and ubiquitous as a graphic artist in entertainment.⁠”
Louise Sandhaus is a graphic designer and faculty at the California Institute of the Arts. She is the founder and co-director ofThe People’s Graphic Design Archive, a crowd-sourced virtual archive that aims to expand, diversify, and preserve graphic design history. Author of Earthquakes, Mudslides, Fires and Riots: California and Graphic Design 1936–1986 and co-author of A Colorful Life: Gere Kavanaugh, Designer Sandhaus is recognized“for her presence and voice in the community as an educator and author — brilliant yet accessible, her work elevates under-recognized designers through stunning publications, insightful storytelling, and an eye toward design in everyday life.⁠”⁠
With themes and issues that expand in numerous creative landscapes to cover a hefty design agenda, from the significance of book design now through the educational challenges to reframe and expand visual research, design ethics and action, the importance of meaningful cultural initiatives for a brand to transition design, the role of design in advocating democracy,this year’s AIGA conference is daring.

Learn more about the speakers here and view the AIGA Design Conference schedule here.
Join AIGA October 20–22, 2022 for the next chapter in design virtually here.

Title: AIGA Design Conference 2022: the award medalists, the hosts, the talks and design’s audacious future - TypeRoom
Chunks: 0,1,2
Just a few days after Inscipt Experimental Type Festival (available to revisit under Replay mode for ticket holders only), another celebration of contemporary design kicks off in search of the creative industry’s next frontier, enter theAIGADesign Conference 2022 October 20-22.
A gathering “for the diverse and ever-changing design community to gather together, inspire and explore how design can and will change the future” for 2022, AIGA Design Conference draws its focus on “Re-Connecting” with its community as the first after a three years hiatus in-person AIGA conference, with a virtual option also available.
Aiming to “celebrate the contributions and impact of design” and searching for design’s next frontiers. AIGA Design Conference 2022 introduces “a new twist to our mainstage” by welcoming three hosts to guide the ticket holders “through the most pressing, cutting edge, and provocative topics impacting design.”
AIGA’s Conference chair akaMATTER’s Rick Griffith, along with Brian Collins of COLLINS,Debbie Millman, andLee-Sean Huang, are the moderators who aim to lead “insightful discussions about the impact of design on our world.”
Bringing together a diverse roster of speakers working in “bold new ways, and exploring how design can build better bridges” AIGA Design Conference 2022 will look past the looking glass addressing “the world’s newest challenges, and learn how we can all make positive progress” through design.
Highlights include the Fireside Chats session and the AIGA Awards Celebration. Hosted by AIGA’s executive director Bennie F. Johnson the Fireside Chats’ theme is the future of design, with guests Audrey Lui, VP, head of design at Lyft,Tim Allen, global head of design at Instacart,Arem Duplessis, Apple’s group creative director and Pepsi’s chief design officer Mauro Porcini.
The recipients of this year’s AIGA Award, are designers and practitioners highly influential in the design industry. This year’s recipients areAndrew Satake Blauvelt,Emily Oberman, andLouise Sandhaus.
Video 3

Blauvelt is a designer, curator, historian, critic, and educator whose practice spans the fields of art and culture. Since 2015, he has served as Director of Cranbrook Art Museum in metropolitan Detroit leading the institution’s transformation into a vibrant and diverse cultural destination and community partner. Having studied and practiced graphic design, Blauvelt has expanded his practice to also include authoring historical research; curating major exhibitions on art, architecture, and design; editorial design for both print and online publishing; conceiving and managing strategic design initiatives; and writing theory and criticism about the field.⁠ AIGA recognizes Blauvelt “for his vast work in the field of art and design in service of the public — a steward of design history, he has redefined the traditional role of the museum in the community and made innovative cultural and educational programming accessible to all.”⁠
Emily Oberman is a multidisciplinary designer whose work spans brand identity, motion graphics, publications, packaging, advertising, and digital. She has been a partner in the New York office of the international design consultancyPentagram design since 2012. ⁠AIGA recognizes Oberman “for imprinting our visual culture with her wit and great fluency of style — highly influential, she is a north star for designers in the business and ubiquitous as a graphic artist in entertainment.⁠”
Louise Sandhaus is a graphic designer and faculty at the California Institute of the Arts. She is the founder and co-director ofThe People’s Graphic Design Archive, a crowd-sourced virtual archive that aims to expand, diversify, and preserve graphic design history. Author of Earthquakes, Mudslides, Fires and Riots: California and Graphic Design 1936–1986 and co-author of A Colorful Life: Gere Kavanaugh, Designer Sandhaus is recognized“for her presence and voice in the community as an educator and author — brilliant yet accessible, her work elevates under-recognized designers through stunning publications, insightful storytelling, and an eye toward design in everyday life.⁠”⁠
With themes and issues that expand in numerous creative landscapes to cover a hefty design agenda, from the significance of book design now through the educational challenges to reframe and expand visual research, design ethics and action, the importance of meaningful cultural initiatives for a brand to transition design, the role of design in advocating democracy,this year’s AIGA conference is daring.

Learn more about the speakers here and view the AIGA Design Conference schedule here.
Join AIGA October 20–22, 2022 for the next chapter in design virtually here.

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-2) the American Institute of Graphic Arts (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of graphic design and visual communication."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.
Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

Honoring design legacies in action. We are so excited to celebrate the 2022 AIGA Award recipients as a part of the AIGA Design Conference in Seattle October 20–22. The AIGA Awards recognize outstanding and unique contributions to the design profession through the AIGA Medal, Steven Heller Prize for Cultural Commentary, and the AIGA Corporate Leadership Award. Stay tuned for the announcement of this year’s honorees!

## Selected list of works
[edit]
Over the course of a career (both independent and professional) that spanned nearly three quarters of a century, Miller produced over 1000 works of art that include internationally recognized corporate branding, illustrations for books, lithographs, drawings, sculptures, and various other projects. Below is a chronological listing of some of his more important and notable work.

## Selected list of works
### At Morton Goldsholl
[edit]
(As chief designer)
*   1976 - Redesign of the branding for 7 Up[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-29)
(As a supporting member of the design team)
*   c.1961 - Motorola.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-31)
rebranding
*   c.1961 - Peace Corps logo  
*   c.1973 - Betty Crocker "Chicken Helper" branding

## Selected list of works
### As an independent artist
[edit]
*   Founders Mosaics - DuSable Museum of African American History

## Later life and death
[edit]
Miller moved into the Smith Village assisted living home in the Morgan Park community in Chicago, where he continued to paint. The dining room at Smith Village was named after him in 2008 when he was 88 years old. Thomas Miller died in his sleep at his home on July 19, 2012.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-32)

## Awards and recognition
[edit]
In 2021, Miller was posthumously awarded the AIGA Medal for "expanding recognition".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Miller_(visual_artist)#cite_note-33)

## [PDF page 1]
THOMAS MILLER
(1920–  2012)
By: Annabell  Lyons

## [PDF page 2]
THOMAS MILLER: PIONEER OF MODERNIST GRAPHIC DESIGN  2
Thomas Miller (1920–  2012)  was a transformative figure in American graphic  
design, best known  for  integrating high-  modernist principles into mainstream  
corporate  identities. Born  in Bristol,  Virginia, Miller  ’s early  life was  marked  by  
the restrictions  of the Jim Crow  South, which forced  him to teach himself the  
fundamentals of art by studying European  masters in secret.  After serving in  
the  Army  during World  War  II, he  moved  to  Chicago, where  he  graduated from  
t h e  R ay -Vogue  School  of  Art  in 1950  as one  of the few African American  
students in the  program.  
Miller  ’s  career  reached  its zenith  during his 35  -year tenure at Morton  
Goldsholl Associates. This firm  was  a  pioneer  in bringing the  Bauhaus aesthetic  
to  Chicago, and Miller became  a  lead designer  who  shaped  the  visual  
landscape of  20th-  century consumer culture. He was a master of the grid  
system, using mathematical precision to create  logos and packaging that were  
both minimalist and universally recognizable.  
Miller  ’s legacy  is defined  by  his "  impeccable craft " and his role as a  
trailblazer. He was one of the first African American designers to be admitted  
into the Society  of Typographic Arts and was posthumously awarded the AIGA  
Medal  i n 2021(  A m e r i ca n  Institute  of  Graphic  Arts). His career  serves  as a bridge  
between  the rigorous  discipline of Swiss design and the vibrant, diverse needs  
of American communication.

## [PDF page 3]
CAREER HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTRIBUTIONS:  3
•Brand Identity: He  played  a critical  role in  
developing the "M" logo for Motorola  and led the  
1970s rebranding of 7-  Up, creating the iconic  red-  
dot-on-green packaging that stood as a masterpiece  
of "The  U n co l a " campaign.
•Minimalist Trademarks: Miller designed numerous  
.  G.  Burroughs  1995.  trademarks for industrial  and consumer companies,  
7-UP (1975)  Dr.  Margaret TDuSable  Museum  of African  American  Historyincluding the Peace Corps,  Storkline Corp, and  
Bauer  & Black, always focusing on distilling  complex  
ideas into essential geometric forms.
•Fine Art & Mosaics: Miller  applied  his  design  
sensibilities to large-scale  mosaics for  the  DuSable  
Museum  of  African  American Histor y  t o  c re a te  
"pixelated"  portraits of historical figures, mixing  
commercial technique  with social advocacy.
Motorola (1955)  Peace Corps  1961

## [PDF page 4]
ICONIC WORK: MOTOROLA & 7-  UP  4
Motorola (1955)  
While  with the team at Morton Goldsholl Associates, Miller  helped  refine  
one of the most enduring symbols in tech:  the "  M" insignia. The design  
utilizes  two peaks to mimic an oscilloscope wavelength, a  nod  to  
Motorola’s roots in  radio and electronics. Miller  applied  a strict geometric  
grid to ensure the logo remained legible whether it was on a tiny circuit  
component or a massive billboard.
7-  Up (1975)  
As the lead designer for the 7-  Up rebranding, Miller  turned  a  soda  
bottle into a modernist icon. He moved away from cluttered,  
traditional  labels to create the bold "Uncola" identity. By  placing  a  
vibrant red circle  against a deep green background and using clean,  
heav y typography, he achieved maximum visual contrast. This  design  
didn't  just sell a drink; it used the g r i d  syste m  to command attention  
on the shelf, defining the brand's look for more than a generation.

## [PDF page 5]
THE GRID  SYSTEM
Thomas Miller  ’s grid system was rooted in  
the  International Typographic  Style (often  
called Swiss Design),  which  he practiced  
during his decades at Morton Goldsholl  
Associates. Rather  than  placing  elements  
by eye,  Miller  used a mathematical  
framework to organize space, ensuring  
that every logo,  line of text, and image  
had a functional  relationship  to one  
another. He forced on 3 things  
Mathematical Ratios/Columns,  
Geometric Abstraction  and  White  
Space/Negative Space.
By  Thomas Miller

## [PDF page 7]
LATE CAREER  &  MOSAICS  7
After decades of defining corporate America, Miller  ’s late-career  
passion for mosaics allowed  him to turn the cold math of the  
grid into something personal and soulful. He found a unique  
rhythm in the meticulous,  meditative process of hand-  painting  
thousands of  tiny  cells within industrial  egg-crate light  
diffusers. For  Miller, these mosaics weren't just  art  they  were a  
way  to catch the light and give permanent, shimmering form to  
the heroes of African American history. This work allowed  him  
to bring his lifetime  of design precision to a higher purpose,  
honoring his community and ensuring its legacy was literally  
built into the architecture  of the city.

## Selected list of works
[edit]
Over the course of a career (both independent and professional) that spanned nearly three quarters of a century, Miller produced over 1000 works of art that include internationally recognized corporate branding, illustrations for books, lithographs, drawings, sculptures, and various other projects. ## [PDF page 1]
THOMAS MILLER
(1920–  2012)
By: Annabell  Lyons

## [PDF page 2]
THOMAS MILLER: PIONEER OF MODERNIST GRAPHIC DESIGN  2
Thomas Miller (1920–  2012)  was a transformative figure in American graphic  
design, best known  for  integrating high-  modernist principles into mainstream  
corporate  identities. Born  in Bristol,  Virginia, Miller  ’s early  life was  marked  by  
the restrictions  of the Jim Crow  South, which forced  him to teach himself the  
fundamentals of art by studying European  masters in secret.  After serving in  
the  Army  during World  War  II, he  moved  to  Chicago, where  he  graduated from  
t h e  R ay -Vogue  School  of  Art  in 1950  as one  of the few African American  
students in the  program.  
Miller  ’s  career  reached  its zenith  during his 35  -year tenure at Morton  
Goldsholl Associates. This firm  was  a  pioneer  in bringing the  Bauhaus aesthetic  
to  Chicago, and Miller became  a  lead designer  who  shaped  the  visual  
landscape of  20th-  century consumer culture. He was a master of the grid  
system, using mathematical precision to create  logos and packaging that were  
both minimalist and universally recognizable.  
Miller  ’s legacy  is defined  by  his "  impeccable craft " and his role as a  
trailblazer. He was one of the first African American designers to be admitted  
into the Society  of Typographic Arts and was posthumously awarded the AIGA  
Medal  i n 2021(  A m e r i ca n  Institute  of  Graphic  Arts). His career  serves  as a bridge  
between  the rigorous  discipline of Swiss design and the vibrant, diverse needs  
of American communication.

## [PDF page 3]
CAREER HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTRIBUTIONS:  3
•Brand Identity: He  played  a critical  role in  
developing the "M" logo for Motorola  and led the  
1970s rebranding of 7-  Up, creating the iconic  red-  
dot-on-green packaging that stood as a masterpiece  
of "The  U n co l a " campaign.
•Minimalist Trademarks: Miller designed numerous  
.  G.  Burroughs  1995.  trademarks for industrial  and consumer companies,  
7-UP (1975)  Dr.  Margaret TDuSable  Museum  of African  American  Historyincluding the Peace Corps,  Storkline Corp, and  
Bauer  & Black, always focusing on distilling  complex  
ideas into essential geometric forms.
•Fine Art & Mosaics: Miller  applied  his  design  
sensibilities to large-scale  mosaics for  the  DuSable  
Museum  of  African  American Histor y  t o  c re a te  
"pixelated"  portraits of historical figures, mixing  
commercial technique  with social advocacy.
Motorola (1955)  Peace Corps  1961

## [PDF page 4]
ICONIC WORK: MOTOROLA & 7-  UP  4
Motorola (1955)  
While  with the team at Morton Goldsholl Associates, Miller  helped  refine  
one of the most enduring symbols in tech:  the "  M" insignia. The design  
utilizes  two peaks to mimic an oscilloscope wavelength, a  nod  to  
Motorola’s roots in  radio and electronics. Miller  applied  a strict geometric  
grid to ensure the logo remained legible whether it was on a tiny circuit  
component or a massive billboard.
7-  Up (1975)  
As the lead designer for the 7-  Up rebranding, Miller  turned  a  soda  
bottle into a modernist icon. He moved away from cluttered,  
traditional  labels to create the bold "Uncola" identity. By  placing  a  
vibrant red circle  against a deep green background and using clean,  
heav y typography, he achieved maximum visual contrast. This  design  
didn't  just sell a drink; it used the g r i d  syste m  to command attention  
on the shelf, defining the brand's look for more than a generation.

## [PDF page 5]
THE GRID  SYSTEM
Thomas Miller  ’s grid system was rooted in  
the  International Typographic  Style (often  
called Swiss Design),  which  he practiced  
during his decades at Morton Goldsholl  
Associates. Rather  than  placing  elements  
by eye,  Miller  used a mathematical  
framework to organize space, ensuring  
that every logo,  line of text, and image  
had a functional  relationship  to one  
another. He forced on 3 things  
Mathematical Ratios/Columns,  
Geometric Abstraction  and  White  
Space/Negative Space.
By  Thomas Miller

## [PDF page 7]
LATE CAREER  &  MOSAICS  7
After decades of defining corporate America, Miller  ’s late-career  
passion for mosaics allowed  him to turn the cold math of the  
grid into something personal and soulful. He found a unique  
rhythm in the meticulous,  meditative process of hand-  painting  
thousands of  tiny  cells within industrial  egg-crate light  
diffusers. For  Miller, these mosaics weren't just  art  they  were a  
way  to catch the light and give permanent, shimmering form to  
the heroes of African American history. This work allowed  him  
to bring his lifetime  of design precision to a higher purpose,  
honoring his community and ensuring its legacy was literally  
built into the architecture  of the city.

Since 1920,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-2) the American Institute of Graphic Arts (AIGA) has awarded medals "to individuals in recognition of their exceptional achievements, services or other contributions to the field of graphic design and visual communication."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_AIGA_medalists#cite_note-3) Below is a **list of AIGA medalists**.
Nine medals were awarded in the 1920s, seven in the 1930s, eight in the 1940s, twelve in the 1950s, ten in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 13 in the 1980s, and 33 in the 1990s. Since 2000, a larger number of medals have awarded; 45 were awarded from 2000 to 2009.

1955, New York, New York
By Glen Helfand
September 11, 2010
Follow Us
FacebookLinkedInPinterestXThreads
_Recognized for her ability to surprise and inform through her poignant communication designs for global brands and arts institutions, and for instilling that skill in others through her teaching._
When it comes to the challenges and complexities of design, Jennifer Morla is a champion of its ability to refocus the way we see the familiar. “How as designers,” Morla wonders, “can we reach out to an audience and make them experience a brand in a more meaningful way? To invite them to re-examine their perception of a company and say, ‘This is Clorox?!’’” She could easily have substituted any number of companies (having worked extensively with Levi’s, Apple Computer, Design Within Reach, Wells Fargo, Herman Miller, among many others) for the well-known cleaning brand. Regardless of client, Morla consistently uses design to open eyes.
“You always have to give them the combo platter: surprise and educate,” she says, punctuated by an engaging laugh. Peruse her portfolio—which contains examples from Morla Design, the studio she founded in San Francisco in 1984—and a focus emerges, centering on elevated standards and a multidisciplinary arsenal of approaches to branding, print, web, packaging, and retail store design. Highlights include poster designs such as a 2009 piece on Iranian dissent featuring lips seemingly sewn shut; packaging, such as a bag for the Discovery Store that creates a shimmering moiré pattern when in use; and books, such as a gorgeous coffee-table tome on the history of Levi’s.

# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
###### AIGA Landor Associates poster, 2003Client: AIGA San Franicsco Chapter; Art director: Jennifer Morla; Designers: Jennifer Morla, Brian Singer.


# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
###### Design Within Reach: Outdoor catalog, 2008Client: Design Within Reach; Art director: Jennifer Morla; Designers: Jennifer Morla, Tina Yuan.


# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
###### United Airlines Hemispheres Magazine cover, 2002Client: Hemispheres Magazine/Pace Communications; Art director: Jennifer Morla; Designers: Jennifer Morla, Hizam Haron; Illustrator: Jennifer Morla.
“The wonderful and humbling part about design is, it’s a big responsibility, as things don’t go away,” she says, referring to the life cycle of design artifacts. “You have a responsibility to make them as good as they can be.”
With an interest in creating works of a lasting nature, she has frequently aligned herself with arts organizations such as New Langton Arts and Capp Street Project in San Francisco and SculptureCenter in New York. Morla explains that “art is always in the background” of what she does, and she maintains a parallel practice of painting large encaustic pieces and creating site-specific installations. Morla’s early experience with motion graphics also factors heavily in her interdisciplinary stance on art: her first job when landing in San Francisco in 1978 was at PBS station KQED, where, as senior designer for on-air and print graphics, she honed her skills by creating concise, moving typography for its broadcasts.
Conceptual art has certainly influenced Morla Design, whose signature style is hard to pin down, with diverse approaches ranging from Swiss austerity for a Michael Mina restaurant menu to Tropicalia in a splashy poster for San Francisco’s Mexican Museum. “I’m not sure there’s a specific stylistic approach,” she admits. “I look for the soul of the brand and let that determine the look and feel.”
Still, Morla welcomes and pursues thoughtful challenges in her meetings with clients: “There’s no project that I’ve taken on that I didn’t think would be the best project I’ve ever done, and it’s exciting to know that the client will go on the ride with me,” she says.

# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
###### United Airlines Hemispheres Magazine cover, 2002Client: Hemispheres Magazine/Pace Communications; Art director: Jennifer Morla; Designers: Jennifer Morla, Hizam Haron; Illustrator: Jennifer Morla.
Morla has captured the essence of numerous clients, but she had the most extensive opportunity with furniture retailer Design Within Reach, for whom she served as chief creative and marketing officer from 2006 until 2008 (she started as creative director in 2005). The position allowed her to more fully express the brand’s spirit and identity, which she accomplished through revamping the format and intention of the regularly published catalogs, making them as much resource as art piece. She filled page spreads with incisive juxtapositions—the classic 1947 Noguchi Table seen next to Eva Zeisel’s coffee table from 1993 is a particularly salient example of Morla’s eye and approach—illustrating a dialogue about design in a mercantile context. As stated in a 2008 interview in _I.D. Magazine_, she wanted to “redefine the concept of catalog from ‘disposable retail mail’ to a vehicle infused with authorship and history.” Her work for the company contributed to its receiving the AIGA Corporate Leadership Award.

# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
AIGA Design ConferenceLearn About the AIGA Medal
**Recognition**
2010 AIGA Medal
**Born**
1955, New York, New York
By Glen Helfand
September 11, 2010
Follow Us
FacebookLinkedInPinterestXThreads
_Recognized for her ability to surprise and inform through her poignant communication designs for global brands and arts institutions, and for instilling that skill in others through her teaching._
When it comes to the challenges and complexities of design, Jennifer Morla is a champion of its ability to refocus the way we see the familiar. “How as designers,” Morla wonders, “can we reach out to an audience and make them experience a brand in a more meaningful way? To invite them to re-examine their perception of a company and say, ‘This is Clorox?!’’” She could easily have substituted any number of companies (having worked extensively with Levi’s, Apple Computer, Design Within Reach, Wells Fargo, Herman Miller, among many others) for the well-known cleaning brand. Regardless of client, Morla consistently uses design to open eyes.
“You always have to give them the combo platter: surprise and educate,” she says, punctuated by an engaging laugh. Peruse her portfolio—which contains examples from Morla Design, the studio she founded in San Francisco in 1984—and a focus emerges, centering on elevated standards and a multidisciplinary arsenal of approaches to branding, print, web, packaging, and retail store design. Highlights include poster designs such as a 2009 piece on Iranian dissent featuring lips seemingly sewn shut; packaging, such as a bag for the Discovery Store that creates a shimmering moiré pattern when in use; and books, such as a gorgeous coffee-table tome on the history of Levi’s.

# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
###### United Airlines Hemispheres Magazine cover, 2002Client: Hemispheres Magazine/Pace Communications; Art director: Jennifer Morla; Designers: Jennifer Morla, Hizam Haron; Illustrator: Jennifer Morla.
“The wonderful and humbling part about design is, it’s a big responsibility, as things don’t go away,” she says, referring to the life cycle of design artifacts. “You have a responsibility to make them as good as they can be.”
With an interest in creating works of a lasting nature, she has frequently aligned herself with arts organizations such as New Langton Arts and Capp Street Project in San Francisco and SculptureCenter in New York. Morla explains that “art is always in the background” of what she does, and she maintains a parallel practice of painting large encaustic pieces and creating site-specific installations. Morla’s early experience with motion graphics also factors heavily in her interdisciplinary stance on art: her first job when landing in San Francisco in 1978 was at PBS station KQED, where, as senior designer for on-air and print graphics, she honed her skills by creating concise, moving typography for its broadcasts.
Conceptual art has certainly influenced Morla Design, whose signature style is hard to pin down, with diverse approaches ranging from Swiss austerity for a Michael Mina restaurant menu to Tropicalia in a splashy poster for San Francisco’s Mexican Museum. “I’m not sure there’s a specific stylistic approach,” she admits. “I look for the soul of the brand and let that determine the look and feel.”
Still, Morla welcomes and pursues thoughtful challenges in her meetings with clients: “There’s no project that I’ve taken on that I didn’t think would be the best project I’ve ever done, and it’s exciting to know that the client will go on the ride with me,” she says.

# 2010 AIGA Medalist: Jennifer Morla
###### United Airlines Hemispheres Magazine cover, 2002Client: Hemispheres Magazine/Pace Communications; Art director: Jennifer Morla; Designers: Jennifer Morla, Hizam Haron; Illustrator: Jennifer Morla.
Morla has captured the essence of numerous clients, but she had the most extensive opportunity with furniture retailer Design Within Reach, for whom she served as chief creative and marketing officer from 2006 until 2008 (she started as creative director in 2005). The position allowed her to more fully express the brand’s spirit and identity, which she accomplished through revamping the format and intention of the regularly published catalogs, making them as much resource as art piece. She filled page spreads with incisive juxtapositions—the classic 1947 Noguchi Table seen next to Eva Zeisel’s coffee table from 1993 is a particularly salient example of Morla’s eye and approach—illustrating a dialogue about design in a mercantile context. As stated in a 2008 interview in _I.D. Magazine_, she wanted to “redefine the concept of catalog from ‘disposable retail mail’ to a vehicle infused with authorship and history.” Her work for the company contributed to its receiving the AIGA Corporate Leadership Award.

Title: Tibor Kalman
Chunks: 4,5,6,7,8
By the 1980s, Kalman was known for being "the 'bad boy' of graphic design" because of his antics and radical consciousness. He believed that award-winning design was only possible when the client was ethical, and frequently called other designers out when he did not agree with their actions. He defined good design as a benefit to everyday life and should be used to increase public awareness of social issues.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-1999-2) Kalman adopted a vernacular style as a way to protest corporate International Style which was the primary design style of the time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-1999-2)

### _Artforum_ and _Interview_ magazines
[edit]
Kalman acted as art director of _Artforum_ magazine in 1987–1988, and as creative director of _Interview_ magazine in 1989–1991,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Cullen-1996-16) collaborating with the same editor, Ingrid Sischy, at both publications. He left his post at _Interview_ after accepting an editor-in-chief position at _Colors_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-23)
Kalman and Oliviero Toscani started the Benetton-sponsored magazine _Colors_ in 1991.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-theguardian-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-26) Two years later, Kalman closed M & Co. and moved to Rome, to work exclusively on _Colors_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Independent-4) Billed as "a magazine about the rest of the world", _Colors_ focused on multiculturalism and global awareness. This perspective was communicated through bold graphic design, multilingualtypography with texts in seven languages,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Munro-2022-17) and juxtaposition of photographs and doctored images, including a series in which highly recognizable figures such as the Pope and Queen Elizabeth were depicted as racial minorities.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Colors-9)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-3)

### _Artforum_ and _Interview_ magazines
From 1981 up until his death, Kalman was married to the illustrator and author Maira Kalman (née Berman).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Alam-2018-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-2003-29) They met while attending NYU.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-2003-29) Together they had two children, Lulu Bodoni and Alex Onomatopoeia.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Alam-2018-28)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-30)
The onset of [non-Hodgkin's lymphoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Hodgkin's_lymphoma "Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma") forced Kalman to leave _Colors_ in 1995 and return to New York. In 1997, he re-opened M & Co. and continued to work until his death on May 2, 1999, in Vega Alta, Puerto Rico.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Colors-9)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-1999-2) Kalman was posthumously awarded the 1999 AIGA medal as the "design profession's moral compass and its most fervent provocateur".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-Heller-3)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Kalman#cite_note-31)

## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
[edit]
In March 2010, Moggridge left IDEO to become director of Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum in New York City, the first person to do so without a museum background. Cooper Hewitt is the only museum in the US devoted exclusively to historic and contemporary design.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-WashPo-14)
Moggridge died of cancer in a hospice in San Francisco on 8 September 2012.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-NYT_Obit-3)
From 1983 to 2010, Moggridge was consulting associate professor in different departments at Stanford University, including the Product Design Program,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Stanford_Design-15) the Center for Work, Technology, and Organization,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Stanford_WTO-16) and the d.school (officially the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Stanford_d.school-17)
Moggridge was Congress Chair for CONNECTING'07, the Icsid World Design Congress held in San Francisco, a role that began in 2000 as he led the effort to prepare a bid that was presented at the 2001 Icsid Congress in Seoul, Korea.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Icsid-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-IDSA-19)
In 2001, Moggridge became a steering committee member at Interaction Design Institute Ivrea in Ivrea, Italy.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Ivrea-20)

## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
In 1993, he was a visiting professor in interaction design at Royal College of Art in London[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-RCA-21) and he was a trustee at the Design Museum in London 1992–1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Cooper-Hewitt-2)_[dead link_] He had been an advisor to the British government on design education in 1974,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-IDSA-19) and a board member at the Copenhagen Institute of Interaction Design.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-CIID-22)
In 2014, Moggridge was posthumously awarded an AIGA Medal.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-23)
Moggridge was given an honorary doctorate from CCA (California College of the Arts) in San Francisco in 2012.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-CCA-10)
In FastCompany's October 2011 issue, Moggridge was profiled as a Master of Design,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-FastCo-24) and named one of the 50 Most Influential Designers in America.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-FastCo_50-25)
In 2010, he was given the Prince Philip Designers Prize.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Design_Council-8)
Moggridge was given a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2009 at the National Design Awards, in a ceremony at the White House, presided over by First Lady Michelle Obama[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-NDA-7)

## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
The Industrial Designers Society of America (IDSA) named Moggridge a Fellow in 2006.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-IDSA-19)
In 1988 Moggridge was named a Royal Designer for Industry by the Royal Society for the encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-RSA-26)
In October 2006, Moggridge published _Designing Interactions_ (The MIT Press, ISBN0-262-13474-8), a 764-page introduction to and history of interaction design comprising 40-plus interviews with designers and entrepreneurs, from Douglas Engelbart to Will Wright to Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Moggridge conducted the interviews, recorded and edited the videos (included with the book on a DVD), and designed the book and the book's website. _BusinessWeek_ named it one of the Best Innovation and Design Books in 2006,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-BW_Best-27) and design commentator Don Norman wrote, "This will be the book—the book that summarizes how the technology of interaction came into being and prescribes how it will advance in the future."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-DI_Reviews-28)
Moggridge followed this in October 2010 with _Designing Media_ (The MIT Press, ISBN0262014858), another compilation of more than 35 interviews with experts in various media, new and old, including Mark Zuckerberg, Chad Hurley, Tim Westergren, Ira Glass, Craig Newmark, Hans Rosling, and DJ Spooky. Again, Moggridge conducted the interviews, wrote the text, and designed the book and the book's website.
Moggridge is a central figure in Gary Hustwit's 2009 documentary on design, _Objectified_.

## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
In 2009, Moggridge directed and produced a short film, _Professor Poubelle_ on YouTube, about Doug Wilde, a Stanford Professor Emeritus who began picking up trash on his daily bike rides up a steep mountain highway.

### Movie title sequences
[edit]
Robert Brownjohn's work on two James Bond title sequences, _From Russia with Love_ and _Goldfinger_, is probably his most widely known achievement. In these he used the technique of projecting moving footage onto the bodies of models and filming the results. The idea of filming projections is one gleaned from the Bauhaus and was used by László Maholy-Nagy in his early constructivist films of the 1920s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-Design_Museum_article_on_Brownjohn-8) The combination of this artistic technique with the style and glamour of the 1960s typify Brownjohn's work. The use of wit and risqué humour, for example the deliberate lining up of a projected shot of a golf putt so that the ball appears to roll down gold painted model Margaret Nolan's cleavage, are also classic Brownjohn devices.
_Goldfinger'_ s title design, photographed by David Watkin cost £5000. Brownjohn also designed the British posters for the film featuring Sean Connery and Honor Blackman over a gold painted Margaret Nolan. A second poster, featuring the characters in a golden hand, was designed for Ireland.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-11) Eventually Saltzman and Brownjohn fell out, and Brownjohn worked on no other Bond films.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-12)
In all, Robert Brownjohn designed four title sequences:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-13)
*   _From Russia with Love_ (1963)  
*   _Goldfinger_ (1964)  
*   _Where the Spies Are_ (1965)  
*   _The Night of the Generals_ (1967)

### Movie title sequences
The most notable work from Brownjohn's post-Bond career is the cover for the 1969 Rolling Stones album _Let It Bleed_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-bleed-3)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-14) He also created moving graphics for Midland Bank and Pirelli between 1966 and 1970. His final piece of graphic design was a poster for the New York Peace Campaign in 1969: an ace of spades playing card is laid on a plain white background with the letters "PE" hastily scribbled to the left of it and a question mark to the right.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-:0-2)
Brownjohn also had a supporting role as a fur coat-clad heavy in Dick Clement's film _Otley_.
Brownjohn died from a heart attack in London on August 1, 1970, a week shy of his 45th birthday.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-bleed-3) He was posthumously inducted into the Art Directors Club Hall of Fame in 1995[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-15) and awarded the AIGA Medal in 2002.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-:1-7)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Brownjohn#cite_note-16)

## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
[edit]
In March 2010, Moggridge left IDEO to become director of Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum in New York City, the first person to do so without a museum background. Cooper Hewitt is the only museum in the US devoted exclusively to historic and contemporary design.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-WashPo-14)
Moggridge died of cancer in a hospice in San Francisco on 8 September 2012.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-NYT_Obit-3)
From 1983 to 2010, Moggridge was consulting associate professor in different departments at Stanford University, including the Product Design Program,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Stanford_Design-15) the Center for Work, Technology, and Organization,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Stanford_WTO-16) and the d.school (officially the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Stanford_d.school-17)
Moggridge was Congress Chair for CONNECTING'07, the Icsid World Design Congress held in San Francisco, a role that began in 2000 as he led the effort to prepare a bid that was presented at the 2001 Icsid Congress in Seoul, Korea.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Icsid-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-IDSA-19)
In 2001, Moggridge became a steering committee member at Interaction Design Institute Ivrea in Ivrea, Italy.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Ivrea-20)
texts.6:
## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
In 1993, he was a visiting professor in interaction design at Royal College of Art in London[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-RCA-21) and he was a trustee at the Design Museum in London 1992–1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Cooper-Hewitt-2)_[dead link_] He had been an advisor to the British government on design education in 1974,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-IDSA-19) and a board member at the Copenhagen Institute of Interaction Design.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-CIID-22)
In 2014, Moggridge was posthumously awarded an AIGA Medal.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-23)
Moggridge was given an honorary doctorate from CCA (California College of the Arts) in San Francisco in 2012.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-CCA-10)
In FastCompany's October 2011 issue, Moggridge was profiled as a Master of Design,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-FastCo-24) and named one of the 50 Most Influential Designers in America.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-FastCo_50-25)
In 2010, he was given the Prince Philip Designers Prize.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-Design_Council-8)
Moggridge was given a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2009 at the National Design Awards, in a ceremony at the White House, presided over by First Lady Michelle Obama[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-NDA-7)
texts.7:
## Early life and education
### Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
The Industrial Designers Society of America (IDSA) named Moggridge a Fellow in 2006.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-IDSA-19)
In 1988 Moggridge was named a Royal Designer for Industry by the Royal Society for the encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-RSA-26)
In October 2006, Moggridge published _Designing Interactions_ (The MIT Press, ISBN0-262-13474-8), a 764-page introduction to and history of interaction design comprising 40-plus interviews with designers and entrepreneurs, from Douglas Engelbart to Will Wright to Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Moggridge conducted the interviews, recorded and edited the videos (included with the book on a DVD), and designed the book and the book's website. _BusinessWeek_ named it one of the Best Innovation and Design Books in 2006,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-BW_Best-27) and design commentator Don Norman wrote, "This will be the book—the book that summarizes how the technology of interaction came into being and prescribes how it will advance in the future."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Moggridge#cite_note-DI_Reviews-28)
Moggridge followed this in October 2010 with _Designing Media_ (The MIT Press, ISBN0262014858), another compilation of more than 35 interviews with experts in various media, new and old, including Mark Zuckerberg, Chad Hurley, Tim Westergren, Ira Glass, Craig Newmark, Hans Rosling, and DJ Spooky. Again, Moggridge conducted the interviews, wrote the text, and designed the book and the book's website.
Moggridge is a central figure in Gary Hustwit's 2009 documentary on design, _Objectified_.
